assumption_register.statement: background conditions C must be made explicit for any implication A=>B used in reasoning

formal.anchor: F=(p,v) where p is the proposition and v represents the current epistemic assessment of that proposition

lexical.anchor: F=(p,v) where p is the proposition and v represents the current epistemic assessment of that proposition

rationale_evidence.anchor: Facts + Evidence -> Reasoning/Logic -> Epistemic Assessment -> Probabilistic Value ... not simply: Facts -> Probability
rationale_evidence.statement: Before assigning a probability to a fact, one must first examine the logical/reasoning structure R:(O_1,O_2,F_1,F_2)->p that supports it and determine how strongly/weakly that reasoning establishes p; only if the relevant regime is probabilistic does one then assign P(p|O_1,O_2,O_3,F_1,F_2,R). The correct sequence is Facts+Evidence -> Reasoning/Logic -> Epistemic Assessment -> Probabilistic Value, not a direct Facts -> Probability jump.

rationale_evidence.anchor: F_1: A with P(A)=0.9 and R: A=>B. The logic tells us the relationship A->B. The probabilistic regime then has to determine how uncertainty propagates ... That is not automatically P(B)=0.9.
rationale_evidence.statement: Logic determines the relationship (A=>B); the probabilistic regime must separately determine how uncertainty propagates through that relationship (P(B|A,...)), which is not automatically equal to P(A). Additional assumptions are required, which is precisely why a logic lens must be applied before a probabilistic lens.

rationale_evidence.anchor: We cannot say: Probability=uncertainty. Probability is one mathematical representation of uncertainty under specified assumptions. ... Two rational observers may therefore have: P_A(p|E,C) != P_B(p|E,C) because their models differ.
rationale_evidence.statement: Probability must not be equated with uncertainty in general; probability is one mathematical representation of uncertainty under specified assumptions. If the assumptions/model change, P1(p|E,C) != P2(p|E,C); consequently two rational observers with the same evidence E and context C but different models can legitimately hold P_A(p|E,C) != P_B(p|E,C) -- same information + different model -> different epistemic state.

## Rationale
Before assigning a probability to a fact, one must first examine the logical/reasoning structure R:(O_1,O_2,F_1,F_2)->p that supports it and determine how strongly/weakly that reasoning establishes p; only if the relevant regime is probabilistic does one then assign P(p|O_1,O_2,O_3,F_1,F_2,R). The correct sequence is Facts+Evidence -> Reasoning/Logic -> Epistemic Assessment -> Probabilistic Value, not a direct Facts -> Probability jump. [S0673] Logic determines the relationship (A=>B); the probabilistic regime must separately determine how uncertainty propagates through that relationship (P(B|A,...)), which is not automatically equal to P(A). Additional assumptions are required, which is precisely why a logic lens must be applied before a probabilistic lens. [S0673] Probability must not be equated with uncertainty in general; probability is one mathematical representation of uncertainty under specified assumptions. If the assumptions/model change, P1(p|E,C) != P2(p|E,C); consequently two rational observers with the same evidence E and context C but different models can legitimately hold P_A(p|E,C) != P_B(p|E,C) -- same information + different model -> different epistemic state. [S0674]

- [S0673] types=['FORMALIZATION'] scope=OBJECT — "A fact need not start as F=true; instead a fact is a pair F=(p,v) of a proposition p and its current, possibly graded, epistemic assessment v (e.g. F_1=("Nexus is version 3.69", 0.85)), where 0.85 does not yet mean probability, only an unresolved/graded epistemic state." (anchor: "F=(p,v) where p is the proposition and v represents the current epistemic assessment of that proposition")
- [S0673] types=['PRINCIPLE', 'ARGUMENT'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Before assigning a probability to a fact, one must first examine the logical/reasoning structure R:(O_1,O_2,F_1,F_2)->p that supports it and determine how strongly/weakly that reasoning establishes p; only if the relevant regime is probabilistic does one then assign P(p|O_1,O_2,O_3,F_1,F_2,R). The correct sequence is Facts+Evidence -> Reasoning/Logic -> Epistemic Assessment -> Probabilistic Value, not a direct Facts -> Probability jump." (anchor: "Facts + Evidence -> Reasoning/Logic -> Epistemic Assessment -> Probabilistic Value ... not simply: Facts -> Probability")
- [S0673] types=['CONCEPT', 'EXTENSION'] scope=OBJECT — "Under the F=(p,v) model, a 'probabilistic fact' is possible: F_i=(p_i,P_i) where P_i=P(p_i | E_i,R_i,F_{<=t}) is the probability conditioned on evidence, reasoning, and prior facts up to time t; but the probability belongs to the state of our determination of the fact, not to the proposition itself." (anchor: "F_i=(p_i,P_i) where P_i=P(p_i | E_i,R_i,F_{<=t})")
- [S0673] types=['EXAMPLE'] scope=OBJECT — "Worked example: 'the server is running Nexus 3.69' is not '85% true' as a proposition; rather, given evidence and reasoning at time t our current assessment of correctness is 0.85, and this can move to 0.97 or drop to 0.20 with new evidence tomorrow without the underlying proposition itself having changed -- only the epistemic state changed." (anchor: "The server is running Nexus 3.69 ... Given the evidence and reasoning available to us at time t, our current assessment that this proposition is correct is 0.85")
- [S0673] types=['DISTINCTION'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Three things must be distinguished: the proposition p itself; the epistemic evaluation of the proposition at time t, E_t(p); and, within a probabilistic regime, P_t(p) as one possible mathematical representation of that evaluation. Hence p != P_t(p) and Knowledge != Probability, though Knowledge may contain probabilistically assessed facts." (anchor: "p != P_t(p) and Knowledge != Probability. But Knowledge may contain probabilistically assessed facts.")
- [S0673] types=['ARGUMENT', 'WARNING'] scope=OBJECT — "Logic determines the relationship (A=>B); the probabilistic regime must separately determine how uncertainty propagates through that relationship (P(B|A,...)), which is not automatically equal to P(A). Additional assumptions are required, which is precisely why a logic lens must be applied before a probabilistic lens." (anchor: "F_1: A with P(A)=0.9 and R: A=>B. The logic tells us the relationship A->B. The probabilistic regime then has to determine how uncertainty propagates ... That is not automatically P(B)=0.9.")
- [S0673] types=['FORMALIZATION', 'CONCEPT'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Proposes a layered pipeline diagram: Observations -> Evidence -> Fact/Proposition -> Logical Structure ('why does this follow?') -> Epistemic Assessment, which then branches into a Deterministic (0/1) or Probabilistic (0...1) realization, both feeding into Knowledge State; 'epistemic assessment' is kept as the more general concept, with the probabilistic value as one regime-specific realization of it." (anchor: "OBSERVATIONS -> EVIDENCE -> FACT/PROPOSITION -> LOGICAL STRUCTURE ... -> EPISTEMIC ASSESSMENT -> (Deterministic 0/1, Probabilistic 0...1) -> KNOWLEDGE STATE")
- [S0673] types=['DISTINCTION'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "In the ideal case E_t(p) in {0,1} (the proposition is fully resolved true or false); in the actual/observed case E_t(p) in (0,1) because available evidence and reasoning do not fully resolve the proposition -- giving precise meaning to 'we try our best but never reach the best', i.e. we move an estimate towards, but generally do not reach, the ideal E_t^*(p)." (anchor: "Ideal Knowledge -> deterministic resolution where possible, while Observed Knowledge -> graded epistemic state where necessary")
- [S0673] types=['OPEN-QUESTION', 'FUTURE-RESEARCH'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Open research question: how to determine the logical strength of reasoning supporting a fact before assigning an epistemic/probabilistic state, comparing formal logic, argumentation theory, Bayesian inference, fuzzy/many-valued logic, evidence theory, and measurement theory; and whether the sequence Proposition -> Reasoning structure -> Epistemic state -> Probability holds universally or some cases require a different ordering." (anchor: "How do we determine the logical strength of the reasoning supporting a fact before assigning an epistemic/probabilistic state to that fact? ... formal logic, argumentation theory, Bayesian inference, fuzzy/many-valued logic, evidence theory, and measurement theory should now be compared.")
- [S0674] types=['CORRECTION'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "The prior Evidence->Reason->Fact chain was too deterministic because it treated each arrow as certain; instead both evidence (E|C,t) and reasoning (R|E,C,t) must themselves be modeled as conditional assessments, not certain steps." (anchor: "We should not model: Evidence -> Reason -> Fact as if each arrow were certain. Instead: E|C,t and R|E,C,t are themselves conditional assessments.")
- [S0674] types=['FORMALIZATION', 'EXAMPLE'] scope=OBJECT — "Evidence is conditional: for proposition p, we have P(E|p,C,t) and P(p|E,C,t); evidence has meaning relative to context, model, source, observation method and time, so E != p and E supports p only conditionally. Example: a server responding on port 8081 is evidence for 'Nexus is running' but not conclusive, since another service, a proxy, stale configuration, a test instance, or an unexpected process could also explain the observation." (anchor: "A server responds on port 8081. That is evidence for: "Nexus is running." but not necessarily conclusive evidence. There could be: another service; a proxy; stale configuration; a test instance; an unexpected process.")
- [S0674] types=['FORMALIZATION', 'EXAMPLE'] scope=OBJECT — "Reasoning is also conditional: an implication A=>B actually depends on background assumptions C={c1,...,cn}, so the real structure is (A and C)=>B, i.e. R(B|A,C) rather than an unconditional A=>B. Example: 'if Nexus 3.69 is running AND this is the production instance AND the requirement applies to this environment, then the system violates requirement R.'" (anchor: "(A and C) => B ... If Nexus 3.69 is running and this is the production instance and the requirement applies to this environment, then the system violates requirement R. The reasoning is therefore: R(B|A,C).")
- [S0674] types=['FORMALIZATION'] scope=OBJECT — "The entire determination is conditional: D(p|E,R,C,t) where p=proposition, E=evidence, R=reasoning structure, C=conditions/context, t=time; probability then enters as P(p|E,R,C,t), which is really P(p|E,model,assumptions,C,t) -- conditional on the reasoning model and its assumptions, not simply P(p|E)." (anchor: "D(p|E,R,C,t) ... P(p|E,R,C,t). But notice something subtle: The probability is conditional on the reasoning model. We are ... saying: P(p|E,model,assumptions,C,t).")
- [S0674] types=['CORRECTION', 'DEFINITION'] scope=OBJECT — "Redefines 'Fact': instead of asserting 'a fact is true' unconditionally, define Fact_t(p|C,R,E) meaning p has been determined as a fact under specified conditions, evidence, and reasoning at time t; this allows Fact_{t1}(p) to hold under one context while Fact_{t2}(p) is later revised when new evidence or changed conditions appear." (anchor: "We should probably stop saying: "A fact is true." and instead investigate: Fact_t(p|C,R,E) meaning: p has been determined as a fact under specified conditions, evidence and reasoning at time t.")
- [S0674] types=['DISTINCTION', 'WARNING'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "There are (at least) four distinct uncertainties that must be kept separate rather than collapsed into a single number too early: evidence uncertainty (reliability of the observation, P(E|p,C)), model/reasoning uncertainty (reliability of the reasoning model, P(R|E,C)), state uncertainty (which underlying state actually exists, P(S|E,C)), and proposition uncertainty (given everything, P(p|E,R,C,t))." (anchor: "Evidence uncertainty P(E|p,C) ... Model/reasoning uncertainty P(R|E,C) ... State uncertainty P(S|E,C) ... Proposition uncertainty P(p|E,R,C,t). These must not be collapsed into one number too early. That is a major research issue.")
- [S0674] types=['FORMALIZATION', 'EXAMPLE'] scope=OBJECT — "A single observation O can be compatible with multiple possible underlying states S1,S2,S3 ("overlapping elements"), so P(Si|O,C) distributes probability mass across them; the extraction process is therefore not a direct mapping O->S but O -> {S1,S2,S3,...} -> conditional assessment -- this is exactly where probability becomes useful." (anchor: "O ~ S1,S2,S3. Therefore: P(Si|O,C) may distribute across them. The extraction process is therefore not: O -> S. It is: O -> {S1,S2,S3,...} -> conditional assessment.")
- [S0674] types=['ARGUMENT', 'WARNING'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Probability must not be equated with uncertainty in general; probability is one mathematical representation of uncertainty under specified assumptions. - [S0674] types=['FORMALIZATION', 'EXTENSION'] scope=THEORY-LEVEL — "Rewrites the full pipeline as fully conditional: observations O_{<=t}, parameterized by context C_t, produce evidence E_t=E(O_{<=t}|C_t); evidence plus prior facts, parameterized by reasoning model M_t and context, produce reasoning R_t=R(E_t,F_{<t}|M_t,C_t); reasoning under context/time yields the determined fact F_t=D(R_t|C_t,t); and under a probabilistic regime, P(F_t|O_{<=t},F_{<t},M_t,C_t)."
